links.note: 431 says the prosperity (பெருக்கம்) of those without arrogance, anger and smallness 'has the quality of பெருமிதம்' (பெருமித நீர்த்து), which Parimelazhagar glosses as eminence. 979 uses the same word for the fault: greatness is 'பெருமிதம் இன்மை' and smallness is riding on it. The pairing shows the word carrying both senses, a dignity that belongs to the prosperity and a conceit that belongs to the person.

431 lists செருக்கு first among the faults whose absence gives prosperity its dignity. 180 names a செருக்கு it approves of, 'வேண்டாமை என்னும் செருக்கு', the pride of not wanting, which yields victory (விறல் ஈனும்); Parimelazhagar there glosses the word as wealth. Read together they separate arrogance from a pride that consists in refusing to covet.

431 names three things to be without, செருக்கு, சினம், சிறுமை, which Parimelazhagar reads as elation, anger and excessive desire, and ties their absence to a ruler's worthy prosperity. 360 names காமம், வெகுளி, மயக்கம் and says pain ends when even their names perish. A closely similar triad is removed for worldly standing in one place and for release in the other.

432 counts 'மாண்பிறந்த மானம்', honour that has gone beyond what is fine, as a fault in a ruler. 384 makes மானம் part of the definition of kingship: 'மறனிழுக்கா மானம் உடையது அரசு'. So the fault in 432 is not honour itself but honour that has left its proper bounds, which is why the verse needs its qualifier.

432 lists 'மாணா உவகை' among a ruler's faults; Parimelazhagar takes it as joy beyond measure. 531 says why such joy is dangerous: the slackness that comes from the elation of great joy (சிறந்த உவகை மகிழ்ச்சியிற் சோர்வு) is worse than excessive anger. 531 supplies the mechanism for the fault 432 only names.

432 calls honour that has passed beyond the fine a fault in a ruler. 1028 says that for one raising his family, idling and minding his மானம் brings ruin (மடிசெய்து மானங் கருதக் கெடும்). Both treat a misplaced sense of honour as a fault, one in the king and one in the head of a house.

433: those ashamed of blame take a fault the size of a millet (தினைத்துணை) as the size of a palmyra (பனைத்துணையாக் கொள்வர்). 104 has the same frame and the same verb for a benefit received: those who know its fruit take a millet's worth of help as a palmyra's. The shared figure magnifies one's own fault in one verse and another's kindness in the other.

433 says the blame-fearing treat a millet-sized fault as palmyra-sized. 965 says even people like a hill are diminished if they do a lowering thing the size of a குன்றி seed. 965 gives the outward fact, that a tiny act does lower the great, which makes the inward magnifying in 433 an accurate estimate and not an exaggeration.

433 describes how those ashamed of blame weigh a small fault of their own. 957 says a fault in the well-born shows up raised high, like the spot on the moon (மதிக்கண் மறுப்போல் உயர்ந்து). 957 adds the public side: in a person of standing a small fault is seen large by others too.

434 calls fault 'அற்றம் தரூஉம் பகை', the enemy that brings ruin, and tells one to guard against it. 421 calls understanding 'அற்றம் காக்கும் கருவி', the tool that guards against ruin, and a fortress enemies can't destroy. The two adjacent chapters use the same word for what is at stake, one naming the inner enemy and the other the inner defence.

434 says fault itself is the enemy that brings ruin. 304 asks whether there is any other enemy (பகையும் உளவோ பிற) than anger, which kills laughter and joy. 304 applies to one named fault the claim 434 makes of fault in general: the real enemy is inside.

434 treats fault as the enemy to guard against. 165 says envy is enough for the envious: even if enemies fail to act, it brings ruin (ஒன்னார் வழுக்கியும் கேடீன்பது). Both say a person's own fault does the work an outside enemy would otherwise have to do.

435: the life of one who doesn't guard before it comes (வருமுன்னர்க் காவாதான்) perishes like straw before fire. 535: one who slipped by not guarding beforehand (முன்னுறக் காவாது இழுக்கியான்) will later grieve over his own error. The same failure is given two outcomes, sudden destruction in 435 and late regret in 535.

435 states the cost of not guarding in advance. 429 states the positive case: those whose understanding guards against what is ahead (எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்) have no affliction that comes to shake them. Parimelazhagar restricts 435 to faults, while 429 speaks of any coming harm, so together they show foresight as one habit across both.

436: if a ruler removes his own fault and can then see others' faults (பிறர்குற்றங் காண்கிற்பின்), what fault attaches to him? 190: if people could see their own faults as they see strangers' (தங்குற்றங் காண்கிற்பின்), what harm would come to living beings? Both are conditional questions built on the same verb, and both make looking at one's own fault the precondition for looking at anyone else's.

549 says that guarding the people and removing wrongdoing (குற்றம் கடிதல்) is no stain on a king but his work. 436 adds an order: he must first remove his own fault (தன்குற்றம் நீக்கி). Parimelazhagar draws the consequence that punishing others' faults without first curbing one's own would itself be a fault.

437: the wealth of one who clings to it without doing what should be done with it (செயற்பால செய்யாது இவறியான்) perishes without lasting. 228 asks whether the hard-eyed who keep what they have and lose it (வைத்திழக்கும்) don't know the joy of giving. Both assume hoarded wealth is lost anyway; 228 adds what the hoarder missed in the meantime.

437 says wealth perishes when its owner does not do the things that ought to be done (செயற்பால செய்யாது ... கெடும்). 466 says one perishes by doing what is unfit and also by not doing what is fit (செய்தக்க செய்யாமை யானுங் கெடும்). The miser of 437 is a case of 466's second half: ruin by omission.

437 says the miser's wealth perishes because he does not do what should be done with it; Parimelazhagar lists these as virtue, increase of wealth and enjoyment. 1006 says one who neither uses his wealth himself nor gives to the deserving (தான்துவ்வான் ... ஈதல் இயல்பிலாதான்) is an ஏதம், a harm, to great wealth. 1006 spells out the two uses left undone and turns the miser himself into the wealth's affliction.

438 says the miserliness called the clinging heart (பற்றுள்ளம் என்னும் இவறன்மை) is not to be counted among any others; Parimelazhagar takes this to mean it exceeds all other faults. 1002 names what lies behind it, the delusion (மருள்) that everything comes by wealth, so that one clings without giving (ஈயாது இவறும்), and gives its result as an inglorious birth. 1002 supplies a cause and a consequence for the fault 438 ranks.

432 lists இவறல் as one of three faults in a ruler, beside excessive honour and excessive joy. 438, on Parimelazhagar's reading, takes it out of any such list as greater than the rest (எற்றுள்ளும் எண்ணப்படுவதொன்று அன்று). Manakkudavar reads 438 differently, as saying miserliness is not to be valued as anything, and on that reading the two verses simply agree.

439 commands: never admire yourself (வியவற்க எஞ்ஞான்றும் தன்னை). 474 gives the outcome for one who doesn't live in accord with others, doesn't know his measure and admires himself (தன்னை வியந்தான்): he perishes quickly. Parimelazhagar connects them in his note on 439, saying that self-admiration keeps one from knowing place, time and strength.

439 ends 'நயவற்க நன்றி பயவா வினை', do not desire a deed that yields no good. 652 ends with the same phrase and extends it: one must always avoid a deed that yields neither renown nor good (புகழொடு நன்றி பயவா வினை). The rule is given in 439 as part of a ruler's guarding against faults and in 652, on Parimelazhagar's reading, as a rule for ministers.

439 forbids admiring oneself at any time. 978 says greatness always bows, while smallness adorns itself in self-admiration (அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து). 978 classifies the act 439 forbids: it is what smallness does.

440: if a ruler can enjoy what he loves without the love being known (காதல் அறியாமை உய்க்கிற்பின்), his enemies' designs come to nothing. 866, from the enemy's side, says one of blinding anger and excessive desire (கழிபெருங் காமத்தான்) is an opponent whose enmity is worth having. Together they show the reasoning: a visible passion is an opening for an enemy, which Parimelazhagar states in his note on 440.

441 tells a ruler to choose, after weighing, the friendship of those who know virtue and are mature in understanding (கேண்மை ... தேர்ந்து கொளல்). 795 tells anyone to examine and take the friendship (நட்பு ஆய்ந்து கொளல்) of those able to make one weep, to rebuke, and to teach the right way. The same instruction, to select friends for their capacity to guide, is given for the king's advisers and for ordinary friendship.

435 says the life of one who does not guard before it comes will burn like straw. 442 tells the ruler to cherish and take as his own those whose nature is to remove the affliction that has come and to guard beforehand against what has not (உறாஅமை முற்காக்கும் பெற்றியார்). The foresight 435 demands of the ruler is, in 442, something he obtains through the people he keeps.

442 describes the people a ruler should keep: they remove the trouble that has come and guard in advance against more. 787 describes friendship in similar terms: it removes what leads to ruin (அழிவினவை நீக்கி), sets one on the path, and shares the suffering when ruin comes. The great adviser and the friend are given the same protective work, though 787 adds a sharing of suffering that 442 does not ask of the adviser.

443 says that cherishing the great and making them one's own (பெரியாரைப் பேணித் தமராக் கொளல்) is the rarest of rare things. 976 uses the same phrase to say where it is absent: the aim 'we will cherish and take the great' (பெரியாரைப் பேணிக் கொள்வேம்) does not exist in the minds of the small. 976 gives one reason for the rarity 443 asserts: the wish itself is missing in small people.

443 calls winning the great as one's own the rarest of rare things (அரியவற்றுள் எல்லாம் அரிது). 781 asks what is as hard to make as friendship (செயற்கரிய யாவுள நட்பின்), and what guard is as hard for an enemy's work to get past. Both rank a bond with others as the hardest thing to obtain, and 781 adds that it is also the strongest protection, which is what chapter 45 goes on to claim for the great.

444: to conduct oneself so that those greater than oneself are one's own is the chief of all strengths (வன்மையுள் எல்லாம் தலை). 891: not slighting the power of the able is the chief of all the safeguards of those who guard themselves (போற்றலுள் எல்லாம் தலை). The two verses use the same ranking formula for the two sides of dealing with the great, winning them as the highest strength and not offending them as the highest protection.

444 places the chief strength in attaching oneself to those greater than oneself; Parimelazhagar adds that this means following their lead. 985 says the strength of those who accomplish things is to bow (ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல் பணிதல்). Both locate strength in deference and not in standing alone.

471 lists the strength of allies (துணைவலி) as one of four strengths to weigh before acting, alongside the deed's, one's own and the opponent's. 444 ranks the strength gained from having the great as one's own above all others (வன்மையுள் எல்லாம் தலை). 444 gives an order of importance to what 471 presents as a list.

445 says a ruler proceeds with his counsellors as his eyes (சூழ்வார் கண்ணாக) and so must choose them with thought. 581 says a ruler should hold spies and the respected treatise as his eyes (மன்னவன் கண்). The king's 'eyes' are advisers in one verse and intelligence plus learning in the other, and in both he sees through something other than himself. This follows Parimelazhagar's reading of 445; Manakkudavar takes its second line differently.

445 tells the ruler to choose his counsellors after deliberation (சூழ்வாரைச் சூழ்ந்து கொளல்), since they serve as his eyes. 462 says nothing is out of reach for those who act after considering a matter with chosen company (தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு தேர்ந்தெண்ணி). Both put the selection of the people one deliberates with before the deliberation itself.

445 says counsellors must be chosen with care because the ruler sees by them. 639 states the cost of choosing badly: a minister at one's side who plots harm (பழுதெண்ணும் மந்திரி) is worse than seventy crore enemies. 639 shows what the care in 445 protects against.

446: against one who can conduct himself as having the worthy for his company (தக்கார் இனத்தனாய்), enemies have nothing left to do. 868 gives the reverse case: one with no good qualities and many faults is without company (இனன் இலன்), and that is a protection to his opponents. Both verses use the word இனம் and both make a ruler's exposure to enemies depend on who stands with him.

446 says enemies can do nothing against one who keeps the company of the worthy. 460 says there is no support greater than good company (நல்லினத்தின் ஊங்கும் துணையில்லை) and nothing that brings more affliction than bad company. 460 states as a general rule what 446 applies to a ruler facing enemies.

447 asks who can ruin those who keep as their own the supporters who rebuke them (இடிக்கும் துணையாரை ஆள்வாரை). 389 says the world rests under the parasol of a king who has the character to bear words bitter to the ear (செவிகைப்பச் சொற்பொறுக்கும்). The two verses describe one arrangement from both sides: advisers who will say hard things and a king who can hear them.

447 values supporters for their rebuking (இடிக்கும்) and says a ruler who has them cannot be ruined. 784 defines friendship by the same act: it is not for laughing but for going ahead to rebuke when one oversteps (மேற்சென்று இடித்தற் பொருட்டு). Rebuke is treated as the purpose of the bond in both statecraft and friendship.

447 speaks of the ruler who keeps rebukers. 638 gives the matching duty of the one beside him: even if the king rejects knowledge and knows nothing himself, the one at his side is bound to tell him what is sound (உறுதி உழையிருந்தான் கூறல் கடன்). 638 extends the idea to the case where the king is not the willing listener 447 assumes.

448: a king without the guard of people who rebuke him will perish even with no one to ruin him (கெடுப்பார் இலானும் கெடும்). 548: a king who is not easy of access and does not examine and do justice will sink and perish of himself (தானே கெடும்). Both describe a king destroyed with no enemy involved, and in both the cause is that he has stopped hearing from others.

448 says a king without rebukers perishes even when there is no one to ruin him. 165 says envy is enough to bring ruin on the envious even if enemies fail to (ஒன்னார் வழுக்கியும் கேடீன்பது). The same pattern, ruin that needs no enemy, appears for an uncorrected ruler and for an envious person.

449: those without capital have no profit (முதலிலார்க்கு ஊதியம் இல்லை), and those without a supporting prop have no stability. 463: the wise do not undertake a deed that loses the capital for the sake of gain (ஆக்கம் கருதி முதலிழக்கும்). Both use the trader's முதல்; 449 makes supporters the capital of a ruler's standing, and 463 warns against risking capital at all.

449 says there is no standing (நிலை) for those without the support of a prop (மதலையாம் சார்பு). 1030 says a family with no good person to stand by and prop it (அடுத்தூன்றும் நல்லாள் இலாத குடி) falls when trouble cuts at its base. The image of a structure that needs a prop is applied to a king in one verse and to a household in the other.

873 says one who, being alone, takes on the enmity of many (பல்லார் பகை கொள்பவன்) is more wretched than the mad. 450 uses the same phrase as its measure: letting go the tie with the good is ten times worse than that (பல்லார் பகை கொளலிற் பத்தடுத்த தீமைத்து). Read together, what 873 treats as an extreme of folly becomes the smaller of two harms in 450.

450 says abandoning one's tie with the good (நல்லார் தொடர் கைவிடல்) is ten times worse than the enmity of many. 800 says to hold close the friendship of the stainless (மருவுக மாசற்றார் கேண்மை) and to be rid of the friendship of the unfit even at a price. 800 gives the same instruction for friendship and adds its other half, which bonds to drop.

450 weighs losing the good against the enmity of many and finds it ten times worse. 816 weighs close friendship with a fool against being a stranger to the wise and finds the second ten million times better (கோடி உறும்). Both rank relationships by a multiplied comparison, and in both the quality of the person outweighs whether the relation is friendly or hostile.
